messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Threat
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

When the night sky over Houston darkened, Zayn, a twenty‑six‑year‑old veterinarian who works long shifts at the city animal clinic, was walking home after a late evening of grooming and administering injections. A shadowy figure stepped out from behind a parked van, demanded a wallet, and brandished a small knife. In the heat of the moment Zayn tried to comply, handing over the wallet without protest, then stepped back to the curb as the attacker ran into the night. The abrupt loss of safety, the cold steel of the weapon, and the scream that followed were seared into Zayn’s memory. In the weeks that followed, Zayn’s sense of well‑being eroded. He no longer felt the same joy in a day’s work; he described a hollow feeling, saying, “I used to be happy, but now I am always miserable.” He began to distrust anyone who offered help, believing that he could not rely on others, and he became convinced that a danger could strike at any moment. These negative appraisals pushed Zayn into a set of coping habits: he would tell himself the robbery was not real or that it wasn’t that bad—magical thinking that minimized the event—while also becoming overly compliant whenever he sensed threat, a fawn response that kept him safe but prevented him from confronting the pain. He started to avoid going out, refusing even to leave the clinic after closing hours. When an ordinary sound—a distant siren or the clatter of a bicycle—reaches his ears, Zayn’s mind abruptly flashes back to the robbery. The memory intrudes without warning, and the scent of gun oil or the metallic tang of a street at dusk can bring the full terror rushing back. When he tries to explain what happened, he finds himself losing the thread and unable to finish the story. Each time this memory surfaces, Zayn instinctively falls back into his magical thinking, trying to convince himself the event never truly happened. The memory also triggers his threat monitoring: he checks behind him, scans the street, and feels an unrelenting alert at home, as if the house itself could be invaded. The ongoing threat vigilance keeps Zayn in a constant state of hyper‑alertness. Every time he hears a rumble of a truck or sees a flicker of movement, he instinctively adopts the same fawn response, staying compliant with anyone who might look hostile. This behavior reinforces the memory of the robbery, as each encounter with perceived danger feels eerily familiar. Moreover, his constant scanning amplifies his negative appraisal that he cannot rely on anyone, solidifying the belief that he must remain on guard at all times. Zayn’s maladaptive strategies now sustain the loop. When he declines to assist a client or chooses to leave the clinic early, he feels a fleeting sense of safety, but the memory of the robbery resurfaces with sharper clarity. His avoidance of public spaces has isolated him from friends and from his partner, who feels increasingly abandoned and frustrated. Each time Zayn stays inside, his perception of safety heightens only to collapse when he hears a noise outside, making the threat feel all the more real. The fawn response keeps him from confronting these patterns, and the magical thinking dulls his awareness of the cycle’s existence. The culmination of these intertwined processes has pushed Zayn to the point of exhaustion. He has missed appointments, his clinic’s client load has dropped, and his partner’s patience has worn thin. Sleep eludes him, and each night the memory returns, punctuated by the familiar scent of fear. The constant threat monitoring has left him emotionally drained. Finally, the accumulation of these stresses prompted Zayn to seek therapy, hoping to reclaim the happiness that once colored his days and to learn whether he could trust others again without feeling perpetually on guard.
